title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: PLAC petitio principii; deny major; contagious depravation
pass_a_gloss: Placeus calls it begging the principle: the argument assumes what is in question. He denies the major; GAR's claim that it was already demonstrated above is nowhere shown and cannot be. Accurately, propagation should be ascribed not to nature alone but to nature's depravation, which is most contagious. Or distinguish the major: concede if the evil is taken as diverse from Adam's first actual and habitual transgression; otherwise deny.
pass_b_english: PLAC. What else is this reason than, as they say, a begging of the principle? For that is brought forward as argument which is plainly the same as what is in question. And so the major is denied: nor is it proved from what the learned man says has already been demonstrated above—for that has nowhere been demonstrated, nor, as I think, can it be demonstrated. Although if we wish to speak accurately, the propagation of corruption ought to be ascribed not to nature alone, but to its depravation: which by its nature is as contagious as can be. The major can also be distinguished: and conceded if the evil be understood as diverse from Adam's first actual and habitual transgression; otherwise denied.
source_text: PLAC. Quid est aliud haec ratio, quam, ut loquuntur, petitio principii? Affertur enim pro argumento illud quod plane idem est cum eo quod versatur in quaestione. itaque negatur major: nec probatur ex eo quod ait vir doctus iam supra demonstratum esse: id enim nusquam demonstratum est, nec, ut arbitror, potest demonstrari. Quanquam si accurate loqui volumus, propagatio corruptionis non soli naturae, sed eius depravationi debet ascribi: quae natura sua contagiosa est ut quod maxime. Potest etiam major distingui: & concedi si malum intelligatur a prima Adae transgressione actuali & habituali diversum; sin minus, negari.

choices.choice: Begs principle; deny major; contagious depravation
